reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes paid OneCoin packages by promising account doubling, substantial token appreciation, and unusually high earnings while urging viewers to join the team immediately. It also presents commissions from direct sales, weaker-side business volume, and generational matching bonuses, making recruitment and downline growth a central path to income rather than merely discussing cryptocurrency. The signup description and closing call to partner with the team provide a direct participation pathway.

opening.argument: Judge the presentation’s projections as projections, not as promises of returns. The account-value example carries a disclaimer saying its price is based solely on predictions and depends on members’ commitment and effort. The three-year growth chart repeats that qualification, while the income slide expressly says income is not guaranteed and may vary with effort, commitment, and skill. The speaker also invites viewers to research the person behind the company. Those qualifications do not prove the forecasts are sound, but they matter when deciding whether the video represents its most striking figures as certain outcomes.

citations.quote: you can do all the research you want on Google about this woman

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution points to a €5,030 package, a €24,000 account-value example, and an invitation to get involved. Those establish that the presentation is promotional. They do not erase the disclaimer printed on the account example itself: the stated price is a prediction whose realization depends on members’ effort. Likewise, the cited invitation does not turn the separately qualified income figures into guaranteed earnings.

citations.quote: Here is the best time and the right time to get involved

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The disclaimers qualify forecasts; they do not change what viewers are being urged to do. The speaker describes paid packages, says accounts will double through splits, and invites viewers to partner with the team now. Most importantly, earnings are tied explicitly to direct sales and a growing team. A warning that income may vary cannot make that recruitment-driven pitch merely market commentary.

opening.argument: There is a substantial teaching component here, not just an earnings pitch. The presentation introduces cryptocurrency trading by comparing it with exchanging conventional currencies, shows a cryptocurrency exchange, and describes lessons delivered through videos, manuals, and quizzes. It also walks through how tokens convert into coins and how an account split is calculated. A judge need not endorse those calculations to recognize an operational explanation of what a prospective participant would receive and how the presented model is said to work. The speaker even says a viewer need not recruit people to make money, so the lesson is not framed solely around building a downline.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution is right that the presentation explains commissions, including payments from team volume. But explaining a compensation plan is also information a prospective participant would need to assess it; that explanation alone does not make every other section a recruitment instruction. The quoted package purchase appears alongside a description of educational materials, and the speaker expressly discusses a route he says does not require recruiting.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Educational material is presented as a benefit of buying a package, not as the video’s endpoint. The speaker explains direct-sale commissions, matching bonuses as a team builds, and payments generated by purchases far down a member’s network. He closes by telling viewers to partner with his team. Saying recruitment is optional does not negate the prominent, explicit downline-income pitch.

opening.argument: The offer is presented with identifiable package tiers and stated benefits, including tokens and cryptocurrency education. The speaker says a package is a one-time purchase without a continuing monthly commitment. Referral commissions and team bonuses are disclosed rather than hidden. That makes it possible to read the video as an aggressive promotion of a product-and-referral business, without treating the existence of a referral structure as proof that a viewer will be cheated. The supplied presentation offers a way to join, but does not itself show a completed payment or demonstrate that the stated educational materials are withheld.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution’s signup link and closing invitation show a sales pathway, but a sales pathway alone does not establish that the offered package delivers nothing. Nor does the account-value example document a realized payout: it describes a hypothetical sequence of splits and values. The stronger reading of the cited evidence is that this is a highly optimistic commercial pitch whose terms and referral incentives are visible to the viewer.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: No completed payment needs to appear for the video to promote the scheme. The offered packages cost money, while the compensation slide prominently promises bonuses from direct sales, weaker-side business volume, and multiple generations. The speaker emphasizes that a purchase by someone a hundred levels below the viewer can generate a bonus, then urges viewers to join his team. Those are the mechanisms the defense’s ordinary-commerce framing leaves out.
